title: How long is a wandering path?

data.source: Richardson (1961), Mandelbrot (1967): the divider method and the dimension of a curve. Checked on simulated paths (R4 with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck force, the worked rotor, and white noise), seeded.

prediction: Counting with a ruler of size sigma, the count falls as sigma to the power -1 for rulers below the path's correlation length and as sigma to the power -2 above it, so coherence is a true length only on the fine side of that crossover.
baseline: The divider method of Richardson (1961) and Mandelbrot (1967): a count that scales as sigma^-D with D = 1 for a smooth curve and D = 2 for a Brownian one.
why: The count behaved as a length for fine rulers and as a Brownian path, with no single length, for coarse ones. So "coherence = arc / sigma" needs the ruler to sit below the path's own correlation length, which R1 to R6 do not supply. Phoenix records the white-noise warning itself (R4, ASSUMPTION) and the study TWO-CLOCKS-MC found that coarse sampling under-reads C; this room adds the exponents on either side of the crossover.
